title: Disclosure of studies, the administrative record, and significant comments
shortTitle: Disclosure of studies, the administrative record, and significant comments
summary: Meaningful comment and judicial review depend on knowing the important materials supporting a proposal and receiving an adequate response to material objections.
notes:
Nova Scotia connects access to the agency’s scientific basis with the ability to provide useful comments. The record for judicial review ordinarily consists of the material before the agency; parties do not receive a fresh merits trial of a regulation whenever it is enforced. That principle makes contemporaneous identification and preservation of relevant material important. The notes attribute the broader critique of informal rulemaking’s diffuse record to William Pedersen.

The subsequent cases distinguish important new information from cumulative material or a later study addressing an issue already fully aired. If genuinely new critical data drive the decision, further disclosure and an opportunity to respond may be necessary. This does not create an endless entitlement to reply to every submission. Agencies also must give reasoned answers to significant comments, with materiality and practical necessity limiting the duty. A comment identifying a decisive flaw or plausible alternative demands different treatment from a bare expression of preference.

The statutory justification and scope of these duties remain contested in the later American Radio Relay discussion. This record describes the assigned line of cases and its internal limits; it does not claim that Nova Scotia requires release of every internal communication or an adjudicatory hearing for every scientific issue.
